author: Staff Writer
title: EDITORIAL: Charlotte Sheriff's Office leaving out info - NewsBreak
text: The Charlotte County Sheriff’s Office has decided to withhold information on arrests that it has provided for years. We don’t like the idea. We question what readers think. The Daily Sun was notified via email recently that the CCSO will no long provide addresses of people they arrest in its online jail log. To some that may not seem like a big deal. We think otherwise. It’s important, we believe, for readers of this newspaper who regularly read our police beat to have some idea where suspected criminals live. People with similar names could be mistaken for a neighbor, for instance. Let’s take a scarier situation. What if the CCSO arrests a sexual predator and they are charged with numerous crimes. And what if that person lived next door and had befriended your children? Wouldn’t you want to know that? We asked about that scenario and the answer we got was not satisfactory. “The arrest location, mugshot, and all other identifying factors should be enough to make sure they are aware,” said Chris Hall, public information officer for the Sheriff’s Office. “If you feel in those cases that the address is needed, you can get it through PRR (a portal used to access information).” We might note that mug shots do not run in police beat and not always in any story that might be written. And, the new process is not the quickest nor easiest way to access that information in our book. Here is the CCSO’s original announcement on its decision: “After some research, I have learned that we are no longer going to be providing the addresses of arrestees on our site, though we will share the arrest locations. Our team decided that we will provide the pertinent information to make the public aware of who the individual is and what charges they face, while at the same time being mindful that some information does not need to be included and has shown that it can create more issues. (In the 9th District, they have eliminated the posting of mug shots as well, which may become the standard eventually). “That being said, the addresses of arrestees are not typically exempt and can be obtained through public records requests when/if needed.” We understand the issues that publishing full addresses can cause. The address may not always accurate or up-to-date. People move, or they say things that aren’t true. That’s why, many years ago, our editors decided to print the name, age and block of the arrestee, not the full address. It gives readers a good idea where this person lives, but does not pinpoint a home. The information, however, is public. And someone with an interest can always log on and look for it themselves. But not anymore. The new database used by the public and media changed this week to its new format. We don’t believe these changes in information were needed. It looks like an attempt to make it more difficult for the public and the media to get information that is public. If you’re a regular reader of the police beat in The Daily Sun and notice some of the information missing, know that we are trying to find ways to give you that same information we reported before. The idea that mug shots may be the next piece of information that may go is surprising. They, also, are part of the public record. We think more information is better. What do you think?
